title: Quebec grocery store believed to be oldest in North America revived with an Italian twist
summary: Quebec City's J.A. Moisan is believed to be the oldest grocery store in North America. It has survived great depressions and uncertain times, but it’s ready for a new beginning once more. New tenants…

image.caption: After announcing its closure in 2025, J.A. Moisan — believed to be North America's oldest grocery store — reopened its doors on Nov. 20. (Sarah-Kate Dallaire/CBC)

blocks.text: Montreal

Quebec City's J.A. Moisan is believed to be the oldest grocery store in North America. It has survived great depressions and uncertain times, but it’s ready for a new beginning once more. New tenants promise to honour the founding family's legacy, but with an Italian twist.
Quebec City's J.A. Moisan is celebrating its 155th anniversary with a new beginning

A 155-year-old institution in Quebec City — believed to be the oldest grocery store in North America — is back in business, reviving a neighbourhood staple that has fed generations of locals and tourists.
"It's probably the oldest grocery store still in operation in North America," said historian Denis Angers.
J.A. Moisan, opened in 1871 by Jean-Alfred Moisan in the city’s Saint-Jean-Baptiste neighbourhood, has weathered two World Wars, the Great Depression and bankruptcy.
“They were able to survive all that period of time," Angers said.
But, after changing hands multiple times over the decades, the store closed in January 2025 under building owner Donna Willett.
"I fell in love with the old building [but] I had no experience [in groceries]," she said.

Not wanting all the effort — and money — she put into the building to go to waste, she decided to “hang on to it for a while” as its new tenants take root and work toward keeping the shop's legacy alive.
A new beginning
J.A. Moisan officially reopened on Friday, entering a new era under tenants Isabelle Di Pilato and her partner Joseph Di Piliato, who moved from France to Quebec City in April.
The seasoned entrepreneur couple did not know about Moisan's history when they found the space to rent, but they now promise to honour the building's legacy.
"People are thanking us, it means a great deal — it’s a tremendous source of moral support," said Isabelle.
Joseph Di Piliato, Isabelle Di Piliato and their daughter Victoria Di Piliato are excited to welcome customers into J.A. Moisan 2.0. (Sarah-Kate Dallaire/CBC)
The couple says they have plenty of ideas for the store, offering a mix of Quebec, French and Italian cultures and flavours.
"You can look forward to surprises, new offerings and things you might otherwise only get to taste in Italy," said Isabelle.
She adds the building will remain “a friendly, very informal, intimate space," a bit like being at home, "but with an Italian twist.”

items: J.A. Moisan, long a Quebec City treasure, takes fresh approach under new ownership

blocks.text: Joseph adds it isn’t just a business, it’s a family affair, too.

“After all, we are immigrants, and the process of immigration itself is a heavy burden … constant uncertainty and a tremendous amount of resilience," he said. "We've invested all we had in this project.

The new business operators say the support has been immensely surprising since they took over the shop, with several locals knocking at the door and peeking through the windows — even on days the store is closed. (Sarah-Kate Dallaire/CBC)
While anxious to take on a business with such a rich history, the couple says they’re incredibly proud and honoured.
“We know how much this means to the people of Quebec … we absolutely don’t want to let you down," said an emotional Isabelle.
"It’s part of your heritage," adds Joseph, teary-eyed.
‘You can go back in time’
In the early days, grocery stores used to sell exclusively dry food, according to historian Angers.
"If you wanted to buy your fish, your meat, you had to go to the markets throughout the city," he said.
He says J.A. Moisan was one of the first supermarkets in Quebec City "where you can find everything under a single roof.”
What really makes the space special, according to Angers, is its "old-time smell" of wood, spices and freshly brewed coffee.
"This is a place where you can stroll, you can discover things, you can go back in time," he said.
The J.A. Moisan grocery store in 1885, the year Jean-Alfred Moisan became the owner of the building. (Courtesy of Clément St-Laurent)
Isabelle says while the grocery section will remain, the couple added chairs and tables for public use.
"It felt like a shame for people to only spend five minutes in such a beautiful space,” Isabelle said.
“It’s much nicer to be able to sit down for a while, have a coffee, or enjoy a bite to eat.”

Asked if she would take down the store's original sign, Isabelle said not only will she keep it, she also added a photo of J.A. Moisan himself “so that he could keep an eye on us."

The couple says they don't want to erase the past, but rather write a future with the store’s history in mind. To that end, they’re planning to bring back bowler hats and vintage aprons "for an old-school feel."
Founder's family feels honoured
Jacques Faguy, the great-grandson of founder Jean-Alfred Moisan, says he is glad the new owners decided to keep his family's name.
Faguy's 97-year-old mother Thérèse Légaré-Faguy, who spent much of her childhood at the store, still lives in the neighbourhood and plans to visit the new shop soon.
He only hopes the family's store and legacy will remain for decades to come.

"We're struggling now to have shops on main streets, [all] cities are struggling to keep and have local merchants," he said, adding he's grateful a staple of the Saint-Jean Baptiste neighbourhood is still standing.
"The store changed, but the name remains.”
